Trial 1 Trial 1 was a randomized, double‑blind, active‑controlled, international, multi‑center clinical trial (NCT#03729362) in patients ≥18 years old diagnosed with LOPD.

Patients were randomized 2:1 to receive POMBILITI (20 mg/kg by intravenous infusion) in combination with Opfolda (260 mg orally for those ≥50 kg or 195 mg orally for those ≥40 kg to <50 kg) or a non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product with placebo every other week for 52 weeks.

The efficacy population included a total of 123 patients of whom 95 (77%) had received prior treatment with U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa or a non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product (ERT‑experienced) and 28 (23%) were ERT‑naïve.
More than two thirds (n=64, 67%) of ERT‑experienced patients had been on ERT treatment for more than 5 years prior to entering Trial 1 (mean of 7.4 years).

Demographics, baseline sitting forced vital capacity (FVC) (% predicted), and 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) were generally similar between the 2 treatment groups (see Table 5 for baseline sitting FVC [percent predicted] values).

The racial groups for the patients consisted of 104 White (85%), 6 Japanese (5%), 6 Other racial group (5%), 4 Asian (3%), 1 Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander (1%), 1 American Indian or Alaska Native (1%), and 1 Black or African American (1%).

Life-threatening hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported in POMBILITI-treated patients.

In clinical trials, 43 (27%) POMBILITI-treated patients experienced hypersensitivity reactions, including 4 (3%) patients who reported severe hypersensitivity reactions and 4 (3%) additional patients who experienced anaphylaxis (fulfilling at least one of the Sampson criteria).
Three of the 4 (2%) patients experiencing anaphylaxis discontinued from the trial [see Clinical Studies (14) ] .
Some patients may require prolonged observation times.
Based on findings from animal reproduction studies, POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda may cause embryo-fetal harm when administered to a pregnant female and is contraindicated during pregnancy.

In a rabbit embryo-fetal development study, great vessel and cardiac malformations were increased in offspring of pregnant rabbits treated with cipaglucosidase alfa‑atga in combination with oral miglustat at 16‑fold and 3‑fold, respectively, the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD) based on plasma AUC exposure.

In a rabbit embryo-fetal development study, great vessel and cardiac malformations were increased in offspring of pregnant rabbits treated with cipaglucosidase alfa‑atga in combination with oral miglustat at 16‑fold and 3‑fold, respectively, the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD) based on plasma area under the plasma concentration-time curve (AUC) exposure.
Verify the pregnancy status in females of reproductive potential prior to initiating treatment with POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda.

Advise females of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment with POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda and for at least 60 days after the last dose [see Use in Specific Populations (8.1 , 8.3 )].

Patients were randomized 2:1 to receive POMBILITI (20 mg/kg by intravenous infusion) in combination with Opfolda (260 mg orally for those ≥50 kg or 195 mg orally for those ≥40 kg to <50 kg) or a non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product with placebo every other week for 52 weeks.

The efficacy population included a total of 123 patients of whom 95 (77%) had received prior treatment with U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa or a non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product (ERT‑experienced) and 28 (23%) were ERT‑naïve.
More than two thirds (n=64, 67%) of ERT‑experienced patients had been on ERT treatment for more than 5 years prior to entering Trial 1 (mean of 7.4 years).

The safety and effectiveness of POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda have been established in pediatric patients aged ≥12 years, weighing ≥10 kg, with LOPD in an ongoing, 52-week, open-label, international, multi-center clinical trial (Cohort 1 of Trial 2).
Cohort 1 included 11 patients, with a mean age at baseline of 14.7 years [see Clinical Pharmacology (12.1) and Clinical Studies (14) ].

The effectiveness in this patient population is supported by population pharmacokinetic analyses, which demonstrate that cipaglucosidase alfa-atga exposure levels in pediatric patients aged ≥12 years are within the range of exposures observed in adult patients.
Additional support of effectiveness is provided by data in pediatric patients aged <12 years (Cohort 2 of Trial 2) [see Clinical Pharmacology (12.3) and ( Clinical Studies (14) ].
The safety profile of POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda in patients aged 12 to <18 years is similar to that observed in adult patients in Trial 1 [see ( Adverse Reactions (6) ] .

In patients with LOPD, excess of glycogen is degraded to hexose tetrasaccharide (Hex4) which is then excreted in urine.
The urinary Hex4 assay measures its major component, glucose tetrasaccharide (Glc4).

Treatment with POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda resulted in reductions of urinary Glc4 concentrations (normalized by urine creatinine and reported as mmol Glc4/mol creatinine) in adult patients with LOPD.

Trial 1 Trial 1 was a randomized, double‑blind, active‑controlled, international, multi‑center clinical trial (NCT#03729362) in patients ≥18 years old diagnosed with LOPD.

Patients were randomized 2:1 to receive POMBILITI (20 mg/kg by intravenous infusion) in combination with Opfolda (260 mg orally for those ≥50 kg or 195 mg orally for those ≥40 kg to <50 kg) or a non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product with placebo every other week for 52 weeks.

The efficacy population included a total of 123 patients of whom 95 (77%) had received prior treatment with U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa or a non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product (ERT‑experienced) and 28 (23%) were ERT‑naïve.
More than two thirds (n=64, 67%) of ERT‑experienced patients had been on ERT treatment for more than 5 years prior to entering Trial 1 (mean of 7.4 years).

Trial 2 Trial 2 (Cohort 1) is an on-going, open-label, international multi center clinical trial (NCT## 03911505) to evaluate safety, pharmacokinetics, efficacy, pharmacodynamics, and immunogenicity in patients 12 to <18 years old and diagnosed with LOPD.
The efficacy of POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda in pediatric patients aged 12 to <18 years is supported by data from Trial 1 and by pharmacokinetic modeling and simulation.

The efficacy population included a total of 11 patients of whom 7 (64%) had received prior treatment with U.S.‑approved alglucosidase alfa or a non U.S.‑approved alglucosidase alfa product (ERT‑experienced) and 4 (36%) were ERT naïve.
Of the 11 patients, 7 were males, baseline mean age was 14.7 years old, and mean age at diagnosis was 7.4 years old for ERT‑experienced patients and 9.5 years old for ERT‑naïve patients.
The racial groups for the patients consisted of 5 White (46%), 3 Japanese (27%), 2 Black or African American (18%), and 1 Asian (9%).

In Cohort 1, pediatric patients aged 12 to <18 years showed an improvement in 6MWD from baseline to Week 52, with a mean (SD) of 456.4 (112.27) meters at baseline, and a mean (SD) change from baseline of 25.4 (29.41) meters.

For sitting percent predicted FVC, patients showed an improvement from baseline to Week 52, with a mean (SD) at baseline of 84.4% (28.49) and a mean (SD) change from baseline of 1.6% (8.28) ( Table 9 ).

In clinical trials, 43 (27%) POMBILITI-treated patients experienced hypersensitivity reactions, including 4 (3%) patients who reported severe hypersensitivity reactions and 4 (3%) additional patients who experienced anaphylaxis (fulfilling at least one of the Sampson criteria).
Three of the 4 (2%) patients experiencing anaphylaxis discontinued from the trial [see Clinical Studies (14) ] .

Based on findings from animal reproduction studies, POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda may cause embryo-fetal harm when administered to a pregnant female and is contraindicated during pregnancy.

In a rabbit embryo-fetal development study, great vessel and cardiac malformations were increased in offspring of pregnant rabbits treated with cipaglucosidase alfa‑atga in combination with oral miglustat at 16‑fold and 3‑fold, respectively, the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD) based on plasma AUC exposure.

In a rabbit embryo-fetal development study, great vessel and cardiac malformations were increased in offspring of pregnant rabbits treated with cipaglucosidase alfa‑atga in combination with oral miglustat at 16‑fold and 3‑fold, respectively, the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD) based on plasma area under the plasma concentration-time curve (AUC) exposure.
Verify the pregnancy status in females of reproductive potential prior to initiating treatment with POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda.

Advise females of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment with POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda and for at least 60 days after the last dose [see Use in Specific Populations (8.1 , 8.3 )].

Investigational NAT for parvovirus B19 (B19) is also performed on pooled samples of all source plasma and the limit for B19 DNA in a manufacturing pool is set not to exceed 10 4 IU/mL.
The manufacturing steps for Nabi-HB are designed to reduce the risk of transmission of viral disease.

diff_lines.text: In patients with LOPD, excess of glycogen is degraded to hexose tetrasaccharide (Hex4) which is then excreted in urine.
The urinary Hex4 assay measures its major component, glucose tetrasaccharide (Glc4).

Treatment with POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda resulted in reductions of urinary Glc4 concentrations (normalized by urine creatinine and reported as mmol Glc4/mol creatinine) in adult patients with LOPD.

In ERT‑experienced patients in Trial 1 [see Clinical Studies (14) ] , the baseline mean urinary Glc4 concentration was 4.6 mmol/mol and 7.2 mmol/mol in the POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda and the non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product with placebo groups, respectively.

The mean percentage (SD) change in urinary Glc4 concentration from baseline to Week 52 was ‑29% (32) and +20% (32) in the POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda and the non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product with placebo groups, respectively.

The mean percentage (SD) change in urinary Glc4 concentration from baseline to Week 52 was -59.5% (19.6).

POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda, is indicated for the treatment of late-onset Pompe disease (lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase [GAA] deficiency) in adults who are not improving on their current enzyme replacement therapy (ERT)) and in pediatric patients 12 years or older.
Safety and effectiveness of POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda have not been established in pediatric patients with late-onset Pompe disease.

The safety and effectiveness of POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda have been established in pediatric patients aged ≥12 years, weighing ≥10 kg, with LOPD in an ongoing, 52-week, open-label, international, multi-center clinical trial (Cohort 1 of Trial 2).
Cohort 1 included 11 patients, with a mean age at baseline of 14.7 years [see Clinical Pharmacology (12.1) and Clinical Studies (14) ].

The effectiveness in this patient population is supported by population pharmacokinetic analyses, which demonstrate that cipaglucosidase alfa-atga exposure levels in pediatric patients aged ≥12 years are within the range of exposures observed in adult patients.
Additional support of effectiveness is provided by data in pediatric patients aged <12 years (Cohort 2 of Trial 2) [see Clinical Pharmacology (12.3) and ( Clinical Studies (14) ].
The safety profile of POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda in patients aged 12 to <18 years is similar to that observed in adult patients in Trial 1 [see ( Adverse Reactions (6) ] .
The safety and effectiveness of POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda have not been established in patients with LOPD <12 years of age.

diff_lines.text: Safety and effectiveness of POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda have not been established in pediatric patients with late-onset Pompe disease.

The safety and effectiveness of POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda have been established in pediatric patients aged ≥12 years, weighing ≥10 kg, with LOPD in an ongoing, 52-week, open-label, international, multi-center clinical trial (Cohort 1 of Trial 2).
Cohort 1 included 11 patients, with a mean age at baseline of 14.7 years [see Clinical Pharmacology (12.1) and Clinical Studies (14) ].

The effectiveness in this patient population is supported by population pharmacokinetic analyses, which demonstrate that cipaglucosidase alfa-atga exposure levels in pediatric patients aged ≥12 years are within the range of exposures observed in adult patients.
Additional support of effectiveness is provided by data in pediatric patients aged <12 years (Cohort 2 of Trial 2) [see Clinical Pharmacology (12.3) and ( Clinical Studies (14) ].
The safety profile of POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda in patients aged 12 to <18 years is similar to that observed in adult patients in Trial 1 [see ( Adverse Reactions (6) ] .
The safety and effectiveness of POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda have not been established in patients with LOPD <12 years of age.

In patients with LOPD, excess of glycogen is degraded to hexose tetrasaccharide (Hex4) which is then excreted in urine.
The urinary Hex4 assay measures its major component, glucose tetrasaccharide (Glc4).

Trial 1 Trial 1 was a randomized, double‑blind, active‑controlled, international, multi‑center clinical trial (NCT#03729362) in patients ≥18 years old diagnosed with LOPD.

Patients were randomized 2:1 to receive POMBILITI (20 mg/kg by intravenous infusion) in combination with Opfolda (260 mg orally for those ≥50 kg or 195 mg orally for those ≥40 kg to <50 kg) or a non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product with placebo every other week for 52 weeks.

The efficacy population included a total of 123 patients of whom 95 (77%) had received prior treatment with U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa or a non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product (ERT‑experienced) and 28 (23%) were ERT‑naïve.
More than two thirds (n=64, 67%) of ERT‑experienced patients had been on ERT treatment for more than 5 years prior to entering Trial 1 (mean of 7.4 years).

Demographics, baseline sitting forced vital capacity (FVC) (% predicted), and 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) were generally similar between the 2 treatment groups (see Table 5 for baseline sitting FVC [percent predicted] values).

Trial 2 Trial 2 (Cohort 1) is an on-going, open-label, international multi center clinical trial (NCT## 03911505) to evaluate safety, pharmacokinetics, efficacy, pharmacodynamics, and immunogenicity in patients 12 to <18 years old and diagnosed with LOPD.
The efficacy of POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda in pediatric patients aged 12 to <18 years is supported by data from Trial 1 and by pharmacokinetic modeling and simulation.

The efficacy population included a total of 11 patients of whom 7 (64%) had received prior treatment with U.S.‑approved alglucosidase alfa or a non U.S.‑approved alglucosidase alfa product (ERT‑experienced) and 4 (36%) were ERT naïve.
Of the 11 patients, 7 were males, baseline mean age was 14.7 years old, and mean age at diagnosis was 7.4 years old for ERT‑experienced patients and 9.5 years old for ERT‑naïve patients.
The racial groups for the patients consisted of 5 White (46%), 3 Japanese (27%), 2 Black or African American (18%), and 1 Asian (9%).

In Cohort 1, pediatric patients aged 12 to <18 years showed an improvement in 6MWD from baseline to Week 52, with a mean (SD) of 456.4 (112.27) meters at baseline, and a mean (SD) change from baseline of 25.4 (29.41) meters.

For sitting percent predicted FVC, patients showed an improvement from baseline to Week 52, with a mean (SD) at baseline of 84.4% (28.49) and a mean (SD) change from baseline of 1.6% (8.28) ( Table 9 ).

In patients with LOPD, excess of glycogen is degraded to hexose tetrasaccharide (Hex4) which is then excreted in urine.
The urinary Hex4 assay measures its major component, glucose tetrasaccharide (Glc4).

Treatment with POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda resulted in reductions of urinary Glc4 concentrations (normalized by urine creatinine and reported as mmol Glc4/mol creatinine) in adult patients with LOPD.

In ERT‑experienced patients in Trial 1 [see Clinical Studies (14) ] , the baseline mean urinary Glc4 concentration was 4.6 mmol/mol and 7.2 mmol/mol in the POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda and the non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product with placebo groups, respectively.

Life-threatening hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported in POMBILITI-treated patients.

In clinical trials, 43 (27%) POMBILITI-treated patients experienced hypersensitivity reactions, including 4 (3%) patients who reported severe hypersensitivity reactions and 4 (3%) additional patients who experienced anaphylaxis (fulfilling at least one of the Sampson criteria).
Three of the 4 (2%) patients experiencing anaphylaxis discontinued from the trial [see Clinical Studies (14) ] .
Some patients may require prolonged observation times.
Based on findings from animal reproduction studies, POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda may cause embryo-fetal harm when administered to a pregnant female and is contraindicated during pregnancy.

In a rabbit embryo-fetal development study, great vessel and cardiac malformations were increased in offspring of pregnant rabbits treated with cipaglucosidase alfa‑atga in combination with oral miglustat at 16‑fold and 3‑fold, respectively, the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD) based on plasma AUC exposure.

In a rabbit embryo-fetal development study, great vessel and cardiac malformations were increased in offspring of pregnant rabbits treated with cipaglucosidase alfa‑atga in combination with oral miglustat at 16‑fold and 3‑fold, respectively, the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD) based on plasma area under the plasma concentration-time curve (AUC) exposure.
Verify the pregnancy status in females of reproductive potential prior to initiating treatment with POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda.

Advise females of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment with POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda and for at least 60 days after the last dose [see Use in Specific Populations (8.1 , 8.3 )].

POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda, is indicated for the treatment of late-onset Pompe disease (lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase [GAA] deficiency) in adults who are not improving on their current enzyme replacement therapy (ERT)) and in pediatric patients 12 years or older.
Trial 1 was a randomized, double‑blind, active‑controlled, international, multi‑center clinical trial (NCT#03729362) in patients ≥18 years old diagnosed with LOPD.
Trial 1 Trial 1 was a randomized, double‑blind, active‑controlled, international, multi‑center clinical trial (NCT#03729362) in patients ≥18 years old diagnosed with LOPD.

Patients were randomized 2:1 to receive POMBILITI (20 mg/kg by intravenous infusion) in combination with Opfolda (260 mg orally for those ≥50 kg or 195 mg orally for those ≥40 kg to <50 kg) or a non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product with placebo every other week for 52 weeks.

The efficacy population included a total of 123 patients of whom 95 (77%) had received prior treatment with U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa or a non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product (ERT‑experienced) and 28 (23%) were ERT‑naïve.
More than two thirds (n=64, 67%) of ERT‑experienced patients had been on ERT treatment for more than 5 years prior to entering Trial 1 (mean of 7.4 years).

Demographics, baseline sitting forced vital capacity (FVC) (% predicted), and 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) were generally similar between the 2 treatment groups (see Table 5 for baseline sitting FVC [percent predicted] values).

Demographics, baseline sitting forced vital capacity (FVC) (% predicted), and 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) were generally similar between the 2 treatment groups (see Table 7 for baseline sitting FVC [percent predicted] values).
Of the 123 randomized patients, 56 were males, baseline mean age was 47 years old (range from 19 to 74 years old), and mean age at diagnosis was 39 years old (range from 1 to 66).

The racial groups for the patients consisted of 104 White (85%), 6 Japanese (5%), 6 Other racial group (5%), 4 Asian (3%), 1 Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander (1%), 1 American Indian or Alaska Native (1%), and 1 Black or African American (1%).
Key efficacy endpoints included assessment of sitting FVC (% predicted) and 6MWD ( Table 5 and Table 6 ).

The ERT‑experienced patients treated with POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda showed a numerically favorable change in sitting FVC from baseline at Week 52 ( Table 5 and Figure 2 ).

Trial 2 Trial 2 (Cohort 1) is an on-going, open-label, international multi center clinical trial (NCT## 03911505) to evaluate safety, pharmacokinetics, efficacy, pharmacodynamics, and immunogenicity in patients 12 to <18 years old and diagnosed with LOPD.
The efficacy of POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda in pediatric patients aged 12 to <18 years is supported by data from Trial 1 and by pharmacokinetic modeling and simulation.

The efficacy population included a total of 11 patients of whom 7 (64%) had received prior treatment with U.S.‑approved alglucosidase alfa or a non U.S.‑approved alglucosidase alfa product (ERT‑experienced) and 4 (36%) were ERT naïve.
Of the 11 patients, 7 were males, baseline mean age was 14.7 years old, and mean age at diagnosis was 7.4 years old for ERT‑experienced patients and 9.5 years old for ERT‑naïve patients.
The racial groups for the patients consisted of 5 White (46%), 3 Japanese (27%), 2 Black or African American (18%), and 1 Asian (9%).

In Cohort 1, pediatric patients aged 12 to <18 years showed an improvement in 6MWD from baseline to Week 52, with a mean (SD) of 456.4 (112.27) meters at baseline, and a mean (SD) change from baseline of 25.4 (29.41) meters.

For sitting percent predicted FVC, patients showed an improvement from baseline to Week 52, with a mean (SD) at baseline of 84.4% (28.49) and a mean (SD) change from baseline of 1.6% (8.28) ( Table 9 ).

Life-threatening hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported in POMBILITI-treated patients.

In clinical trials, 43 (27%) POMBILITI-treated patients experienced hypersensitivity reactions, including 4 (3%) patients who reported severe hypersensitivity reactions and 4 (3%) additional patients who experienced anaphylaxis (fulfilling at least one of the Sampson criteria).
Three of the 4 (2%) patients experiencing anaphylaxis discontinued from the trial [see Clinical Studies (14) ] .
Some patients may require prolonged observation times.
Based on findings from animal reproduction studies, POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda may cause embryo-fetal harm when administered to a pregnant female and is contraindicated during pregnancy.

In a rabbit embryo-fetal development study, great vessel and cardiac malformations were increased in offspring of pregnant rabbits treated with cipaglucosidase alfa‑atga in combination with oral miglustat at 16‑fold and 3‑fold, respectively, the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD) based on plasma AUC exposure.

In a rabbit embryo-fetal development study, great vessel and cardiac malformations were increased in offspring of pregnant rabbits treated with cipaglucosidase alfa‑atga in combination with oral miglustat at 16‑fold and 3‑fold, respectively, the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD) based on plasma area under the plasma concentration-time curve (AUC) exposure.
Verify the pregnancy status in females of reproductive potential prior to initiating treatment with POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda.

Advise females of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment with POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda and for at least 60 days after the last dose [see Use in Specific Populations (8.1 , 8.3 )].

Trial 1 Trial 1 was a randomized, double‑blind, active‑controlled, international, multi‑center clinical trial (NCT#03729362) in patients ≥18 years old diagnosed with LOPD.

Patients were randomized 2:1 to receive POMBILITI (20 mg/kg by intravenous infusion) in combination with Opfolda (260 mg orally for those ≥50 kg or 195 mg orally for those ≥40 kg to <50 kg) or a non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product with placebo every other week for 52 weeks.

The efficacy population included a total of 123 patients of whom 95 (77%) had received prior treatment with U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa or a non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product (ERT‑experienced) and 28 (23%) were ERT‑naïve.
More than two thirds (n=64, 67%) of ERT‑experienced patients had been on ERT treatment for more than 5 years prior to entering Trial 1 (mean of 7.4 years).

Demographics, baseline sitting forced vital capacity (FVC) (% predicted), and 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) were generally similar between the 2 treatment groups (see Table 5 for baseline sitting FVC [percent predicted] values).

Trial 2 Trial 2 (Cohort 1) is an on-going, open-label, international multi center clinical trial (NCT## 03911505) to evaluate safety, pharmacokinetics, efficacy, pharmacodynamics, and immunogenicity in patients 12 to <18 years old and diagnosed with LOPD.
The efficacy of POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda in pediatric patients aged 12 to <18 years is supported by data from Trial 1 and by pharmacokinetic modeling and simulation.

The racial groups for the patients consisted of 5 White (46%), 3 Japanese (27%), 2 Black or African American (18%), and 1 Asian (9%).

In Cohort 1, pediatric patients aged 12 to <18 years showed an improvement in 6MWD from baseline to Week 52, with a mean (SD) of 456.4 (112.27) meters at baseline, and a mean (SD) change from baseline of 25.4 (29.41) meters.

In clinical trials, 43 (27%) POMBILITI-treated patients experienced hypersensitivity reactions, including 4 (3%) patients who reported severe hypersensitivity reactions and 4 (3%) additional patients who experienced anaphylaxis (fulfilling at least one of the Sampson criteria).
Three of the 4 (2%) patients experiencing anaphylaxis discontinued from the trial [see Clinical Studies (14) ] .
Some patients may require prolonged observation times.
Based on findings from animal reproduction studies, POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda may cause embryo-fetal harm when administered to a pregnant female and is contraindicated during pregnancy.

In a rabbit embryo-fetal development study, great vessel and cardiac malformations were increased in offspring of pregnant rabbits treated with cipaglucosidase alfa‑atga in combination with oral miglustat at 16‑fold and 3‑fold, respectively, the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD) based on plasma AUC exposure.

Verify the pregnancy status in females of reproductive potential prior to initiating treatment with POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda.

Advise females of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment with POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda and for at least 60 days after the last dose [see Use in Specific Populations (8.1 , 8.3 )].

In patients with LOPD, excess of glycogen is degraded to hexose tetrasaccharide (Hex4) which is then excreted in urine.
The urinary Hex4 assay measures its major component, glucose tetrasaccharide (Glc4).

Treatment with POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda resulted in reductions of urinary Glc4 concentrations (normalized by urine creatinine and reported as mmol Glc4/mol creatinine) in adult patients with LOPD.

In ERT‑experienced patients in Trial 1 [see Clinical Studies (14) ] , the baseline mean urinary Glc4 concentration was 4.6 mmol/mol and 7.2 mmol/mol in the POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda and the non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product with placebo groups, respectively.

Trial 2 Trial 2 (Cohort 1) is an on-going, open-label, international multi center clinical trial (NCT## 03911505) to evaluate safety, pharmacokinetics, efficacy, pharmacodynamics, and immunogenicity in patients 12 to <18 years old and diagnosed with LOPD.
The efficacy of POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda in pediatric patients aged 12 to <18 years is supported by data from Trial 1 and by pharmacokinetic modeling and simulation.

The efficacy population included a total of 11 patients of whom 7 (64%) had received prior treatment with U.S.‑approved alglucosidase alfa or a non U.S.‑approved alglucosidase alfa product (ERT‑experienced) and 4 (36%) were ERT naïve.
Of the 11 patients, 7 were males, baseline mean age was 14.7 years old, and mean age at diagnosis was 7.4 years old for ERT‑experienced patients and 9.5 years old for ERT‑naïve patients.
The racial groups for the patients consisted of 5 White (46%), 3 Japanese (27%), 2 Black or African American (18%), and 1 Asian (9%).

In Cohort 1, pediatric patients aged 12 to <18 years showed an improvement in 6MWD from baseline to Week 52, with a mean (SD) of 456.4 (112.27) meters at baseline, and a mean (SD) change from baseline of 25.4 (29.41) meters.

For sitting percent predicted FVC, patients showed an improvement from baseline to Week 52, with a mean (SD) at baseline of 84.4% (28.49) and a mean (SD) change from baseline of 1.6% (8.28) ( Table 9 ).

Based on findings from animal reproduction studies, POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda may cause embryo-fetal harm when administered to a pregnant female and is contraindicated during pregnancy.

In a rabbit embryo-fetal development study, great vessel and cardiac malformations were increased in offspring of pregnant rabbits treated with cipaglucosidase alfa‑atga in combination with oral miglustat at 16‑fold and 3‑fold, respectively, the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD) based on plasma AUC exposure.

diff_lines.text: POMBILITI is indicated, in combination with Opfolda, for the treatment of adult patients with late-onset Pompe disease (lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase [GAA] deficiency) weighing ≥40 kg and who are not improving on their current enzyme replacement therapy (ERT).

POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda, is indicated for the treatment of late-onset Pompe disease (lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase [GAA] deficiency) in adults who are not improving on their current enzyme replacement therapy (ERT)) and in pediatric patients 12 years or older.
In patients with LOPD, excess of glycogen is degraded to hexose tetrasaccharide (Hex4) which is then excreted in urine.
The urinary Hex4 assay measures its major component, glucose tetrasaccharide (Glc4).

Treatment with POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda resulted in reductions of urinary Glc4 concentrations (normalized by urine creatinine and reported as mmol Glc4/mol creatinine) in adult patients with LOPD.

In ERT‑experienced patients in Trial 1 [see Clinical Studies (14) ] , the baseline mean urinary Glc4 concentration was 4.6 mmol/mol and 7.2 mmol/mol in the POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda and the non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product with placebo groups, respectively.

In Trial 1, treatment with POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda resulted in reductions of urinary Glc4 concentrations (normalized by urine creatinine and reported as mmol Glc4/mol creatinine) in adult patients with LOPD.

In ERT‑experienced patients [see Clinical Studies (14) ] , the baseline mean urinary Glc4 concentration was 4.6 mmol/mol and 7.2 mmol/mol in the POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda and the non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product with placebo groups, respectively.

The mean percentage (SD) change in urinary Glc4 concentration from baseline to Week 52 was ‑29% (32) and +20% (32) in the POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda and the non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product with placebo groups, respectively.

In Trial 2 [see ( Clinical Studies (14) )] , treatment with POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda resulted in reductions of urinary Glc4 concentrations (normalized by urine creatinine and reported as mmol Glc4/mol creatinine) in pediatric patients 12 to <18 years old with LOPD, consistent with reductions observed in adults.
The mean percentage (SD) change in urinary Glc4 concentration from baseline to Week 52 was -59.5% (19.6).

Cipaglucosidase alfa-atga is expected to be metabolized into small peptides and amino acid via catabolic pathways.

Life-threatening hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported in POMBILITI-treated patients.

In clinical trials, 43 (27%) POMBILITI-treated patients experienced hypersensitivity reactions, including 4 (3%) patients who reported severe hypersensitivity reactions and 4 (3%) additional patients who experienced anaphylaxis (fulfilling at least one of the Sampson criteria).
Three of the 4 (2%) patients experiencing anaphylaxis discontinued from the trial [see Clinical Studies (14) ] .
Some patients may require prolonged observation times.
Based on findings from animal reproduction studies, POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda may cause embryo-fetal harm when administered to a pregnant female and is contraindicated during pregnancy.

In a rabbit embryo-fetal development study, great vessel and cardiac malformations were increased in offspring of pregnant rabbits treated with cipaglucosidase alfa‑atga in combination with oral miglustat at 16‑fold and 3‑fold, respectively, the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD) based on plasma AUC exposure.

Verify the pregnancy status in females of reproductive potential prior to initiating treatment with POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda.

Advise females of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment with POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda and for at least 60 days after the last dose [see Use in Specific Populations (8.1 , 8.3 )].

Patients were randomized 2:1 to receive POMBILITI (20 mg/kg by intravenous infusion) in combination with Opfolda (260 mg orally for those ≥50 kg or 195 mg orally for those ≥40 kg to <50 kg) or a non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product with placebo every other week for 52 weeks.

The efficacy population included a total of 123 patients of whom 95 (77%) had received prior treatment with U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa or a non-U.S.-approved alglucosidase alfa product (ERT‑experienced) and 28 (23%) were ERT‑naïve.

The efficacy of POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda in pediatric patients aged 12 to <18 years is supported by data from Trial 1 and by pharmacokinetic modeling and simulation.

The efficacy population included a total of 11 patients of whom 7 (64%) had received prior treatment with U.S.‑approved alglucosidase alfa or a non U.S.‑approved alglucosidase alfa product (ERT‑experienced) and 4 (36%) were ERT naïve.
Of the 11 patients, 7 were males, baseline mean age was 14.7 years old, and mean age at diagnosis was 7.4 years old for ERT‑experienced patients and 9.5 years old for ERT‑naïve patients.
The racial groups for the patients consisted of 5 White (46%), 3 Japanese (27%), 2 Black or African American (18%), and 1 Asian (9%).

In Cohort 1, pediatric patients aged 12 to <18 years showed an improvement in 6MWD from baseline to Week 52, with a mean (SD) of 456.4 (112.27) meters at baseline, and a mean (SD) change from baseline of 25.4 (29.41) meters.

The safety and effectiveness of POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda have been established in pediatric patients aged ≥12 years, weighing ≥10 kg, with LOPD in an ongoing, 52-week, open-label, international, multi-center clinical trial (Cohort 1 of Trial 2).
Cohort 1 included 11 patients, with a mean age at baseline of 14.7 years [see Clinical Pharmacology (12.1) and Clinical Studies (14) ].

The effectiveness in this patient population is supported by population pharmacokinetic analyses, which demonstrate that cipaglucosidase alfa-atga exposure levels in pediatric patients aged ≥12 years are within the range of exposures observed in adult patients.
Additional support of effectiveness is provided by data in pediatric patients aged <12 years (Cohort 2 of Trial 2) [see Clinical Pharmacology (12.3) and ( Clinical Studies (14) ].
The safety profile of POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda in patients aged 12 to <18 years is similar to that observed in adult patients in Trial 1 [see ( Adverse Reactions (6) ] .
The safety and effectiveness of POMBILITI in combination with Opfolda have not been established in patients with LOPD <12 years of age.
